title: Safety on the first day
lines: Welcome to the workshop, Ben. Before you start, I need to explain the safety rules.
Of course. What do I need to wear?
You must always wear safety glasses and special shoes. You can get them in the store room.
Only when you move heavy boxes. Never wear gloves near the drilling machine.
OK. What do I do if there is an accident?
Press the red button on the wall. It stops all the machines. Then call me.
Thank you. I will be careful.

title: The quality problem
lines: Have you seen the figures for last week? Almost eight percent of the parts were rejected.
Eight percent? That's double the usual rate. Do we know why?
Most of the faulty parts came from the night shift, and nearly all of them were slightly too long.
So it could be the machine settings rather than the material.
That's my guess. A new operator started two weeks ago, and I don't think anyone showed him how to calibrate the cutter properly.
Then it's a training issue. Can you spend a night with him this week?
I'll do it on Wednesday. I'll also put a checklist next to the machine, so that it's checked at the start of every shift.
Good. Let's look at the numbers again in a fortnight.

title: Automating the line
lines: I've read your proposal for the robotic cell. It's impressive, but I have some reservations.
I expected as much. Is it the cost?
Partly. Half a million is a lot for a plant of our size. But what really concerns me is flexibility. We change products every few weeks.
That was true of the previous generation of robots, which took days to reprogram. These can be taught a new task in a couple of hours by an operator, not a specialist.
And what happens to the six people who currently do that job?
Nobody would be laid off. Two would be retrained to supervise the cell, and the rest would move to final assembly, where we're permanently short-staffed.
That makes it easier to sell to the workforce. What about the payback period?
Just under three years, assuming volumes stay as they are. If they grow as forecast, closer to two.

q.a: Apart from the cost, she is worried about flexibility, because the plant changes products every few weeks.

title: The limits of simulation
lines: You've been rather outspoken about what you call the cult of simulation. Isn't that biting the hand that feeds you?

Not at all. I use these tools every day. My quarrel is with the unquestioning faith they inspire. A coloured stress plot looks so authoritative that people forget it's merely the consequence of whatever assumptions were fed in.
Garbage in, garbage out, in other words.
Quite, but with a twist. The garbage is now beautifully rendered. A hand calculation that is wrong tends to look wrong. A simulation that is wrong looks exactly like one that is right.
So what would you have young engineers do?
Estimate the answer before they press the button. If the software disagrees with a rough calculation by a factor of ten, one of them is mistaken, and it pays to find out which.
I'd call it insurance. The tool is superb. It simply shouldn't be the only thing in the room that understands the problem.

q.q: What exactly does the engineer criticise?
q.a: Not the tools themselves but the blind faith in them: an impressive plot makes people forget it only reflects the assumptions that were entered.

q.q: Why is a wrong simulation more dangerous than a wrong hand calculation?
q.a: Because a wrong hand calculation tends to look wrong, whereas a wrong simulation looks exactly like a correct one.

q.q: What habit does she recommend?
q.a: Estimating the answer with a rough calculation before running the software, and investigating if the two differ greatly.

title: Charging at home
lines: I've just ordered an electric car, and I need a charger in my garage. Is that complicated?
Not usually. First I have to check how much power your house has contracted and what condition the panel is in.
A charger can use as much electricity as the rest of the house put together. If the oven and the charger are on at the same time, the main switch could trip.
So do I have to pay for more power?
Not necessarily. I can install a device that measures what the house is using and reduces the charging speed automatically when demand is high.
That sounds sensible. How long does the car take to charge?
With a seven-kilowatt charger, about eight hours from empty, so overnight is ideal. And if you have a night tariff, it costs roughly a third of what you'd pay for petrol.

q.a: The contracted power and the condition of the panel, because a charger can use as much electricity as the rest of the house.

title: After the audit
lines: I've gone through the energy audit, and there are some easy wins, plus one finding that's rather more worrying.
Let's start with the bad news.
The power factor of the plant is poor, around nought point seven. The utility has been charging you a penalty for reactive energy every month, and nobody seems to have noticed.
How much are we talking about?
Close to nine thousand euros a year. A capacitor bank would bring it down to almost nothing and would pay for itself in about fourteen months.
That's a straightforward decision. And the easy wins?
The compressors run all weekend, although the factory is empty. A simple timer would save six percent of your annual bill. And a third of the motors are oversized for what they actually drive.
It would be, so I wouldn't replace them now. Fit variable speed drives to the four largest and change the rest as they wear out.

q.q: What is the worrying finding and what does it cost?
q.a: The plant's power factor is poor, about 0.7, so the utility charges a penalty for reactive energy of nearly nine thousand euros a year.

q.q: What solution does he propose for it?
q.a: Installing a capacitor bank, which would almost eliminate the penalty and pay for itself in about fourteen months.

q.q: What are the 'easy wins' and what does he advise about the motors?
q.a: A timer to stop the compressors at weekends, saving six percent; and for oversized motors, fitting variable speed drives to the four largest and replacing the rest as they wear out.

title: Who pays for the grid?
lines: You've described the way we pay for electricity networks as a quiet injustice. That's a strong phrase.
I stand by it. Most of what a grid costs is fixed; the wires have to be there whether you use them or not. Yet we charge for them largely by the kilowatt-hour.
Which seems fair enough: use more, pay more.
It was, until households started generating their own power. Someone with solar panels buys far less from the grid, and so contributes far less to its upkeep, while still relying on it every evening.
And the shortfall is made up by everybody else.
Precisely, and everybody else tends to be those who rent, or who simply can't afford panels. In effect, the less well-off are subsidising the better-off.
So you'd penalise people for going green?

Hardly. I'd charge for the connection according to the capacity you require, and for the energy separately. Solar would remain attractive. It would merely stop being a way of passing the bill to your neighbour.

q.q: What mismatch does the speaker see in how networks are paid for?
q.a: Most grid costs are fixed, since the wires must exist anyway, but users are charged mainly per kilowatt-hour consumed.

q.q: Why does he call the system unjust?
q.a: Solar owners buy less from the grid and pay less for its upkeep while still depending on it, so the shortfall falls on those who rent or cannot afford panels: the poorer subsidise the richer.

q.q: What reform does he suggest?
q.a: Charging for the connection according to the capacity each user requires, and for the energy separately.

title: A difficult client
lines: You look worried. Is it the Henderson account again?
Yes. He called three times this morning. He's changed the specifications again, and he still expects delivery on the same date.

title: Feedback for a new manager
lines: I wanted to catch up on how your first three months as team leader have gone.
Honestly? Harder than I'd anticipated. I used to be good at my job. Now I spend my days in meetings and I feel as if I produce nothing.
That's an extremely common reaction. You're measuring yourself by your old job. Your output is no longer the drawings you make; it's what your team delivers.
I do understand that in theory. In practice, when I see someone struggling, I end up doing the work myself, because it's quicker.
Quicker today, certainly. But next month they'll bring you the same problem, and the month after.
So I should let them get it wrong?
Within reason, yes. Ask questions that lead them to the answer instead of handing it over. It takes longer at first, and it pays off enormously.
I'll try. It goes against every instinct I have.
I know. That's precisely why so few people do it well.

title: The counter-offer
lines: I gather you've handed in your notice. I won't pretend I'm not disappointed.
It wasn't an easy decision, and I'd rather you heard my reasons from me than through the grapevine.
I appreciate that. Is it the money? Because I've been authorised to match whatever they're offering.
That's generous, but it rather proves my point. I asked for a review eighteen months ago and was told there was nothing in the budget. Apparently there is, provided I threaten to leave.
That's a fair criticism, and I shan't insult you by denying it.
It isn't only the salary, in any case. The new role involves building a team from scratch. Here, I'd be waiting for someone to retire.
Then I won't stand in your way. For what it's worth, the door stays open.
Thank you. I mean to leave things in good order: everything will be documented before I go.

title: Giving up the car
lines: Is it true you've sold your car? I never thought I'd see the day.

Neither did I. But I sat down and worked out what it was costing me: insurance, parking, repairs, the lot. It came to over four thousand a year, for something that sat outside the house ninety-five percent of the time.
But how do you manage? Surely it's a nuisance.
Less than you'd imagine. I cycle to work, which takes about the same time as driving once you count the parking. For anything further, there's the train.
And when you really need one? A trip to the mountains, say?
I rent one for the weekend. Even doing that once a month, I'm spending a fraction of what I used to.
I'm not sure I could do it. I'd miss the freedom.
That's what I assumed. What I've actually noticed is the freedom of not having to worry about it.

q.q: What made the man decide to sell his car?
q.a: He calculated that it cost over four thousand a year in insurance, parking and repairs, while it sat unused ninety-five percent of the time.

q.a: She thinks she would miss the freedom a car gives; he has found freedom in not having to worry about owning one.

title: The clutter of things
lines: Your book argues that our homes have become warehouses. Aren't you overstating it?
If anything, I'm understating it. The average household contains several times as many objects as it did two generations ago, and a whole industry now exists to rent us space for what won't fit.
Yet people seem perfectly happy to keep buying.
Happy at the moment of purchase, certainly. The pleasure is real, but it's remarkably short-lived, whereas the object stays, demanding to be stored, dusted, insured and, eventually, disposed of.
So your advice is to throw it all out?

No, and I've little patience with the fashionable minimalism that turns owning nothing into a competitive sport. My point is more modest. Before acquiring something, ask what it will cost you in attention, not just in money.
And has that worked in your own home?
Imperfectly. My weakness is books, and I've long since given up pretending they count as an exception.

q.q: What evidence does the author give that homes have become 'warehouses'?
q.a: Households hold several times as many objects as two generations ago, and an entire industry rents out storage space for what does not fit.

q.q: What does she recommend, and what does she reject?
q.a: She rejects fashionable minimalism as a competitive sport; she simply recommends asking what an object will cost in attention, not just money, before acquiring it.

title: A cooking disaster
lines: How was your dinner party on Saturday?
Don't ask. It was a complete disaster from start to finish.

title: Running a restaurant
lines: People imagine that owning a restaurant is about cooking. How much of your week do you actually spend at the stove?
Perhaps a third, if I'm lucky. The rest goes on suppliers, staff rotas and paperwork. Nobody warns you that you're opening a small logistics company that happens to serve dinner.
Margins, without a doubt. Out of every ten euros a customer spends, about three go on ingredients, three on wages and another three on rent and energy. What's left is the profit, in a good month.
That leaves very little room for error.
None whatsoever. One quiet week or a broken fridge, and the month is gone. That's why so many places close within two years.
Because on a Saturday night, when the room is full and everything comes together, there's nothing like it. It's irrational, I admit. Most worthwhile things are.

q.a: Only about a third at the stove; the rest goes on suppliers, staff rotas and paperwork, like running a small logistics company.

title: The cult of the ingredient
lines: Menus these days read like maps. Every carrot comes with the name of its farm. Is that information, or theatre?
A little of both. There's a genuine story behind it: good produce matters more than technique, and chefs spent decades ignoring that.
But the pendulum has swung absurdly far. I've been served a single tomato, sliced, with a lecture on the soil it grew in. At some point, somebody has to actually cook.
Isn't restraint a virtue, though? Letting the ingredient speak for itself?

It's a virtue when it's a choice, and an excuse when it's a habit. It takes more skill, not less, to know that a perfect peach needs nothing. But that judgement is rare, and the fashion has given a great many mediocre kitchens permission to do very little and charge a great deal.
You don't sound like a fan.
On the contrary, I love the idea. I simply mistrust anything that becomes compulsory.

title: Youth academies
lines: Your club is famous for its academy. How many of the boys who join at twelve actually make it as professionals?
Fewer than one in a hundred. And I think we have a duty to be honest about that from day one, with the boys and especially with the parents.
That must be a difficult conversation.

It is, because every family is convinced theirs is the exception. But the damage done by false hope is far worse. I've seen sixteen-year-olds released with no qualifications and no idea who they are without football.
So what do you do differently?
School comes first, and I mean that literally: if their marks drop, they don't train. We also bring former players in to talk about what happened after they were let go.
Oddly enough, no. The ones with real ambition work harder, and the others leave with something to fall back on. Either way, we've done right by them.

q.q: What statistic does the coach give, and what does she conclude from it?
q.a: Fewer than one in a hundred boys become professionals, so the club has a duty to be honest with them and their parents from the start.

q.q: What harm has she seen false hope cause?
q.a: Sixteen-year-olds released with no qualifications and no sense of who they are without football.

q.q: What does the academy do differently?
q.a: School comes first: if marks drop, they don't train. Former players also come to talk about life after being released.

gaps.s: I think we have a ___ to be honest about that from day one.
I've seen sixteen-year-olds ___ with no qualifications.
The others leave with something to fall ___ on.

title: The art of commentary
lines: You've commentated on more than two thousand matches. What separates a good commentator from a merely competent one?
Silence, oddly enough. The beginner is terrified of it and fills every second with statistics. The craftsman knows that when a stadium erupts, the best thing he can possibly say is nothing at all.
Television must make that easier than radio.

Easier, and more dangerous. On radio you are the listener's eyes, so you must paint the picture. On television the picture is already there, and the temptation is to describe what everyone can perfectly well see.
Context and feeling. Why this pass matters, what this player went through to be here. And, very occasionally, a phrase that fits the moment so exactly that people repeat it for decades.
Can those be prepared in advance?
The ones that are prepared invariably sound it. The lines that last are the ones that escape before you've had time to polish them.

q.q: What does the commentator consider the mark of a master?
q.a: Knowing when to stay silent: beginners fill every second with statistics, but when the stadium erupts the best comment is none at all.

q.q: Why is television 'easier and more dangerous' than radio?
q.a: On radio you must paint the picture for the listener; on television the picture is already there, so the temptation is to describe what viewers can already see.

q.q: What does he say about memorable phrases?
q.a: They cannot be prepared: prepared lines always sound prepared, and the ones that last come out spontaneously before he has time to polish them.

gaps.s: The ___ knows that when a stadium erupts, the best thing he can possibly say is nothing at all.
The ___ is to describe what everyone can perfectly well see.
The ones that are prepared ___ sound it.
